taxonomy.note: Accepted name; F. texensis and F. americana var./subsp. texensis are synonyms.

evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Fraxinus albicans and lists Texas within its native range.
Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list includes F. albicans; UT Plant Resources Center also documents naturally occurring Texas ash in north Hays County.
Travis County — a wild-provenance collection documents F. albicans in Travis County above Collier Hollow.
Williamson County — a county environmental/archaeological survey describes Texas ash as prevalent in the historic/natural vegetation of the Limestone Cut Plain.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Do not collapse older F. texensis / F. americana var. texensis records into a separate learner taxon; Kew treats them as synonyms of F. albicans. User iNaturalist observations support field/photo coverage but are not needed for the range decision.

morphology.look_here_first: Once you know it is an ash, go to the lower leaflet surface and the samara: Texas ash usually has a glaucous white-reticulate waxy underside, relatively small fruit body, and a wing that is terminal or only slightly decurrent down the seed body.
diagnostic_traits: deciduous small-to-medium ash of rocky limestone slopes, bluffs and canyons
opposite branching and odd-pinnate leaves, usually 5–7 leaflets
leaflets relatively short/broad; margins entire to distally crenulate or crenulate-serrate
abaxial leaflet surface characteristically glaucous with a dense white-reticulate wax overlay; hairs may also occur
leaf scar depressed-obovate with a shallowly concave/notched upper margin and somewhat flaring sides
samara body about 1 cm long; wing terminal or only slightly decurrent on distal quarter
gray bark becoming furrowed with interlocking flattened ridges

confusers.separator: Priority Hays County comparison. Green ash has larger fruit bodies and the wing runs much farther down the body; Texas ash has glaucous/waxy leaflet undersides and a more terminal wing.
Mexican ash usually has 3–5 leaflets with coarser sharp distal serration and may mix 3-winged fruits among normal 2-winged fruits.
White ash has a deeply notched U-shaped leaf scar surrounding the bud and is primarily an eastern-Texas/eastern-North-American species.
